one_liner: Caffeine-style concurrent Go cache (adaptive W-TinyLFU): 10-34x hashicorp/golang-lru throughput at 25-100% reads; slower on pure writes.
what_it_does: Otter is an in-process, generic, concurrent bounded cache for Go, modeled on Java's Caffeine. You build it from an otter.Options struct (MaximumSize, or MaximumWeight plus a Weigher; ExpiryCalculator; RefreshCalculator; OnDeletion; StatsRecorder; Executor) and call GetIfPresent/Set/Invalidate, or Get(ctx, key, loader) for load-through with deduplicated concurrent loads. On top of what golang-lru offers it adds per-entry variable expiry, async refresh-ahead, bulk loading, Compute/ComputeIfAbsent, stats, Hottest/Coldest iterators and gob-based save/load to a file. It is not a drop-in: the method names differ, and eviction weighs frequency as well as recency, so it is not LRU.
how_it_is_fast: The hash table is a fork of puzpuzpuz/xsync's MapOf, a CLHT-style (Cache-Line Hash Table) design with 64-byte buckets of 5 entries and SWAR meta-byte probing, so Get does no memory writes and takes no locks. Policy bookkeeping follows BP-Wrapper: reads go into a lossy striped ring buffer (the stripe count grows when contention is detected) and writes into a bounded growable MPSC queue, and both are replayed in batches under one eviction mutex taken with TryLock, so readers never wait on the policy lock. By contrast, golang-lru takes an exclusive sync.RWMutex Lock on every Get to move the entry to the front. Eviction is adaptive W-TinyLFU (admission window plus segmented main space, a 4-bit count-min sketch and hill-climbing window sizing), expiry uses a hierarchical timing wheel, and node structs are code-generated per feature set so options you don't use add no per-entry memory.
when_to_use: Read-heavy in-process caches shared by many goroutines on multi-core machines, where golang-lru's global lock on Get is the bottleneck (first-party: 34x at 100% reads, 27x at 75/25, 21x at 50/50).

Bounded caches whose access pattern is unknown or shifts between recency- and frequency-biased, where the adaptive W-TinyLFU window beats plain LRU hit rates on the project's trace simulations (S3, DS1, P8, OLTP, Glimpse, mixed).
When you want Caffeine's feature set in Go: per-entry variable TTL, loader dedupe to limit stampedes, background refresh-ahead, weight-based bounds, stats counters, and deletion callbacks.
Generic keys of any comparable type (hashed with maphash.Comparable) and any value type, from hundreds to millions of entries (the eviction benchmark covers capacities from 100 to 1,000,000).
when_not_to_use: Pure-write or update-heavy workloads: at 100% writes otter measured 2.32M ops/s vs golang-lru's 3.23M, behind theine, ristretto, sturdyc, gcache and ttlcache too; the docs themselves list extreme write-heavy loads as the exception.

When the size cap must hold at every instant (tiny caches, or entries that pin scarce resources): with the default async Executor, a tight Set loop pushed a MaximumSize=2 cache to 1,027 entries (issue #171). The maintainer's fix is a synchronous Executor, which moves the eviction work back onto the caller.

Low-contention or single-goroutine use, or small insert-only caches. The gains come from contention; in the insert-only eviction benchmark golang-lru was faster at capacity 100 (266.6 vs 307.5 ns/op), though otter was faster at 10K and 1M.

Hot paths built on Compute with slow callbacks: Compute holds a hash-table bucket lock while the function runs, and open issue #177 reports heavy mutex delay in drainBuffers under frequent Compute (v2.2.1, root cause not yet found).
Toolchains older than Go 1.24, or projects that cannot track new Go releases: the README says only the two most recent Go minor versions are supported.

integration.dependencies: none at runtime beyond the Go standard library (the only direct requirement in go.mod is stretchr/testify, for tests); the slog logger plugin is a separate module (plugin/pslog)
integration.min_toolchain: Go 1.24 (go.mod `go 1.24.0`; uses maphash.Comparable and runtime.AddCleanup). Only the two newest Go minor versions are supported; CI runs Go 1.25.x, plus a 32-bit job on 1.24.x.
integration.platforms: pure Go, so any GOOS/GOARCH in principle. CI runs Linux (ubuntu-latest) plus a 32-bit build; the GOARCH=wasm build was fixed in v2.3.0. Published benchmarks exist only for darwin/arm64 (Apple M1 Pro).
integration.thread_safety: Safe for concurrent use. Hash-table reads are lock-free, writes lock one bucket, and policy updates are applied in batches under a single eviction mutex. Compute* holds a bucket lock during the callback, and loaders must not modify the cache.
integration.drop_in_for_baseline: partial: both are generic in-process caches, but the API differs (Add becomes Set returning (V, bool), Get becomes GetIfPresent, Peek becomes GetEntryQuietly, Remove becomes Invalidate, Purge becomes InvalidateAll, Len becomes EstimatedSize). Keys() is an iterator in unspecified order, not oldest-to-newest. Eviction is W-TinyLFU rather than LRU, and the size bound is soft by default.

gotchas: Policy state is only eventually consistent with the map: eviction and expiry reordering run in batches on a goroutine started through the Executor (default `go fn()`), so EstimatedSize can exceed MaximumSize for a while. Pass a synchronous Executor if you need strict bounds, as the project's own hit-ratio simulator does.
Get(ctx, key, loader) works like singleflight: under a burst of concurrent Gets the loader can still run more than once for the same key (issue #152). A fix PR (#184) has been open since 2026-06-25.

Weights are computed once, on write, and never recomputed; they only decide whether the cache is over capacity, not which entry is evicted. Zero weight or an expiry of math.MaxInt64 is the documented way to pin an entry.

When expiry is enabled, a cleanup goroutine ticks once per second. It is stopped by a runtime.AddCleanup finalizer or by an explicit StopAllGoroutines (needed under synctest, issue #158). SaveCacheTo/LoadCacheFrom use encoding/gob, so K and V must be gob-encodable.
pick_this_over_siblings_when: go-sieve and golang-fifo also report large wins over golang-lru with SIEVE-style policies; pick otter when you also need Caffeine-style features (variable TTL, loader dedupe, refresh-ahead, weights, stats) and an adaptive policy that holds up on both recency- and frequency-biased traces. Caffeine itself is the JVM original that otter's design and benchmark are ported from.
verified_claims_summary: The numbers come from the project's own Go port of Caffeine's GetPutBenchmark: 8 goroutines (-cpu=8), with a 32,768-entry cache pre-filled from a scrambled Zipf over about 10.9K string keys, so every Get hits and every Set is an update with no eviction. Run once on an Apple M1 Pro (darwin/arm64) with an unrecorded Go toolchain, otter reached 106.4M ops/s at 100% reads vs 3.14M for hashicorp/golang-lru v2 (about 34x), about 27x at 75/25, 21x at 50/50 and 10x at 25/75, while golang-lru was about 1.4x faster at 100% writes (3.23M vs 2.32M ops/s).
status_note: v2.3.0 was released 2025-12-22 and main's last commit is 2025-12-23, but the maintainer was still answering issues in 2026 and bug reports and a fix PR (#184) are open; Apache-2.0, pure Go with no runtime dependencies, and the README lists users including Grafana, Centrifugo and FrankenPHP.
